methods.notes: Match the 0xfe32 service UUID, then pick the timer by its address from the owner's exported record. A 0xfe32 device whose GATT table lacks 00006c71-fe32-4f58-8b78-98e42b2c047f is either a hub or a timer in its bootloader; do not send it control frames.

mac_prefixes.notes: IEEE assigns 44:67:55 to Orbit Irrigation (registries/ieee-oui.tsv), and the timer addresses quoted in ljmerza's message catalogue (and the device id inside its captured protobuf frames) carry it. It covers Orbit's whole catalogue, Wi-Fi controllers and hubs included, so it ranks a device as "made by Orbit", not as this spec.

identification.notes: The 0xfe32 service is what ljmerza's firmware-recovery scanner matches. The B-hyve BH1 hub advertises it too, and so does a timer stuck in its bootloader. wxfield's key-extraction notes say the XD advertises the local name "ASR" (not corroborated elsewhere, so not used as a matcher). In practice a client knows its timers by the MAC address in the owner's exported record.

device.name: Orbit B-hyve Bluetooth Hose and XD Timers
device.notes:
Battery-powered valve timers that screw onto an outdoor tap (HT25, HT31) or feed two to four outlets (the "XD" HT32A and HT34/HT34A). The B-hyve phone app drives them directly over BLE, and an optional Wi-Fi hub (BH1) bridges them to the Orbit cloud. Every timer on one account mesh shares one AES-128 "network key" that the cloud generated when the first device was set up; the BLE link is useless without it.
CLOUD DEPENDENCE: the key and, for the HT25-0000 family, two 16-bit mesh ids come from the owner's Orbit account. The owner exports them once (see setup); after that every command and status read in this spec is local BLE and works with the WAN down. A client that has never been given the key cannot talk to the timer, and nothing in this document recovers a lost key without the cloud or the vendor app.
Two wire families share one GATT service and one cipher:
  * HT25-0000 (the original single-outlet hose timer, firmware 0041 and
    0085): a binary "mesh" message, frame magic 0x10, needs a seven-step
    init on every connection and the timer's own mesh id in every frame.
  * Everything else seen so far (HT25G2-0001, HT25A-0001, the bare
    HT25-0001, HT31-0001, HT32A-0001, HT34A-0001, HT34-0001): protobuf
    messages in a CRC-checked inner wrapper, frame magic 0x11.
The routing rule both clients use: hardware string starting HT25 and ending "-0000" is the mesh family; every other HT25*, HT31*, HT32* and HT34* is the protobuf family. The hardware string comes from the owner's account record; nothing in the advertisement says which family a timer is.
The upstream authors warn that a firmware update may change the protocol, and that HT25A-0001 fw0098 behaves differently (see its entity). Hub units (BH1-0001) advertise the same service but have no valve and are not covered.

openness.notes: No vendor publication. Recovered by the ljmerza and wxfield projects from HCI captures of the vendor app and from analysis of the app; the two agree on GATT layout, handshake, keystream, frame and the XD start/stop messages. The HT25-0000 mesh format is from ljmerza only.

exclusivity.recovery: Close the B-hyve app (force-stop it) so it releases the timer's single BLE session, then connect.

pairing.notes: No link-layer pairing or bonding (ljmerza observed nothing written to the host's bond table and no MAC filtering). Security is the mesh key and the AES session handshake in `initialization`. The battery timers take one central at a time; the vendor app holding the session is the usual cause of silent failures.

credentials.notes: The key is not exchanged over BLE and is not derived from the handshake; the handshake only fixes the per-session nonce and counters. A 00006c76-fe32-4f58-8b78-98e42b2c047f write of the key was tried upstream and refused ("write not permitted") on every unit; do not write it.
stored_on_device: HT25-0000: own mesh device id and hub (server bridge) mesh device id
Watering programs, rain delay, controller mode, clock

factory_reset.effect: Not covered by either source. Whether a reset clears the mesh membership and key on the timer, and what button sequence does it, is not established here.

cloud.local_alternative: None for a mesh that has never been exported: the key exists only in the account and in the vendor app's storage. On a rooted Android phone the key can be read from the B-hyve app's cached mesh response (ljmerza docs/network-key-extraction.md, option 3) without contacting the cloud. Once exported, nothing here needs the cloud again.

methods.description: The owner signs in to their own Orbit account once and copies what the timer needs into the local client. ljmerza's integration does this with two REST calls (base https://api.orbitbhyve.com/v1): POST /session with the account e-mail and password returns an API token; GET /devices lists the timers (hardware_version, mac_address, mesh_id, num_stations); GET /meshes/{mesh_id} (newer accounts: /network_topologies/{mesh_id}, also /networks/{mesh_id}) returns the mesh record whose network_key (or ble_network_key) is the base64 AES key and whose devices[] list maps each timer's device_id to its ble_device_id. The requests carry an "orbit-app-id" header; ljmerza sends a browser User-Agent because Orbit's firewall rejects one containing "HomeAssistant".

hub_mesh_device_id.notes: HT25-0000 only. The ble_device_id of the mesh's bridge (bridge_device_id). Absent when the mesh has no hub; ljmerza then sends 0 and reports that the timer still initialises.

mesh_device_id.notes: HT25-0000 only. The timer's ble_device_id from the mesh record's devices[] entry (fallback: the number after the dash in the device record's "reference"). A 16-bit value, written little-endian as the first two bytes of every mesh frame.

network_key.notes: The mesh's AES-128 key: 16 bytes, delivered base64 by the cloud; store as 32 hex characters. Shared by every timer on the mesh. Treat it like a password: it opens every valve on the account and decrypts captured traffic.

methods.name: Owner exports the mesh key once

steps.action: Set the timer up in the B-hyve app on the owner's account, if that has not been done.

Sign in to the account once (or read the app's cache on a rooted phone) and export, per timer, the BLE address, hardware string, mesh network key and, for HT25-0000, the timer's and the hub's mesh device ids.
steps.expect: A 32-hex-character key and the per-timer record, stored in the local client.

steps.action: Decline firmware updates in the vendor app if local control matters; both upstream projects were built against the firmware listed in device.testing.

setup.notes: The timer is first set up with the B-hyve app and an Orbit account; that is when the mesh and its network key are created. A local client then needs, per timer: its BLE address, its hardware string (which picks the wire family), the mesh network key, and for HT25-0000 its own mesh device id and its hub's mesh device id. The upstream integration reads all of it from the account once and stores it; no later step touches the cloud. Re-export after adding a timer or re-creating the account (the key is regenerated only then; it is not rotated on its own, per ljmerza's notes).

rejoin.notes: BLE only, nothing to rejoin. A new local client needs only the exported key and ids; the timer does not know or care which central connects.

testing.notes: Not driven against hardware by this project. Everything below is transcribed from two open-source clients whose authors report end-to-end actuation on their own units (HT25-0000 fw0041/fw0085, HT25G2-0001 fw0111, HT25A-0001 fw0098, HT31-0001 fw0058, HT32A-0001 and HT34A-0001 fw0107). The cipher vectors in protocol_details were computed by this project with an invented key and checked by scripts/test_orbit_bhyve_ble_spec.py; the inner-message CRC was also checked against plaintext frames published in ljmerza's message catalogue.

entities.name: Zone 1
entities.notes: Write-only state: the device reports the running station only in a protobuf status (payload_formats.ProtobufStatus), which no format block can describe, so read it with get_status. The device times the run itself.

entities.name: Zone 2
entities.notes: stop_watering stops whichever zone is running; there is no per-zone stop.

entities.name: Valve
entities.notes: HT25A-0001 fw0098 (hardware-verified upstream, 2026-09-14) ignores the requested run time and always runs its default 1800 s, so the CLIENT must send controller_off when the requested time is up, and then controller_auto if programs should keep running. Never send stop_watering to this model: it restarts a 30-minute run.

entities.name: Valve
entities.notes: Each command needs the seven-frame mesh init earlier in the same connection (protocol_details.ht25_mesh.init_sequence).

entities.name: Battery voltage
entities.notes: Arrives on every connection as the reply to init step 3, so a separate poll is rarely needed.

evidence.documentation_review: Read 2026-10-25: ljmerza/orbit-bhyve-ble at 70b3c90 (code and docs) and wxfield/Orbit_B-Hyve_4Port_Controller at 0bfd0f9. Both implement the same handshake, keystream and 0x11 frame. The stop frame's trailer 80 03 computed from the trailer rule equals the constant wxfield's client sends. The inner CRC was checked against four published plaintext requests. knobunc/ha-orbit-bhyve-ble, cited upstream as a third reference, returned HTTP 451 and was not read.
evidence.open_questions: Whether the device verifies the outer trailer (ljmerza says mismatches are dropped; wxfield's client sent a fixed 80 04 trailer on every start frame, which matches no start frame under the rule); the device's maximum run time; the HT25-0000 countdown scale; which init steps are really required; the factory reset.

dfu_mode.notes: A timer stuck in its bootloader (HT25-0000 after a failed update blinks white about every 2 s) still advertises 0xfe32 and exposes 6c72 and 6c73 but NOT 6c71. ljmerza documents re-flashing such a unit (docs/firmware-recovery.md, verified on two HT25-0000 fw0085 units); that transfer protocol is not transcribed here.

enter.notes: The vendor app's update path is not documented by either source.

image.notes: Images are downloaded per hardware model from the Orbit cloud by the vendor app; ljmerza's recovery tool fetches the same image with the owner's login.

helpful_urls.description: Announcement thread (2026-10-10) with owner reports per model.

initialization.notes: Subscribe BEFORE the handshake write; ljmerza found the device may stay silent otherwise. Every reply in this spec arrives here.

initialization.description: Session handshake, fresh per connection, whose bytes cannot be fixed data. Write 20 random bytes C (byte 11 forced to 0x00, as the vendor app does), then read 20 bytes D back. D[0:4] must be non-zero and D[4:20] all zero, or the handshake failed. Compose S = D[0:4] || C[4:20]: nonce = S[0:12]; host-to-device counter = uint32 LE S[12:16]; device-to-host counter = uint32 LE S[16:20]. See protocol_details.envelope and the test vector there.

HT25-0000 only: the seven-frame mesh init in protocol_details.ht25_mesh.init_sequence, sent encrypted, before EVERY watering command (the upstream client re-runs it per actuation because a command on a stale session is acknowledged and silently ignored). The protobuf family needs no init.

Ht25Status.description: HT25-0000 device-status reply (mesh message 2), decrypted. Header [mesh id LE16][type][02 40] then seven payload bytes.

fields.description: Offset 5: 0x01 idle, 0x04 watering (0x00 off, 0x03 rain delay per upstream's mesh constants).
fields.name: state

fields.description: Offsets 6-7, uint16 LE, remaining time in 1/64-second ticks (upstream hypothesis fitted to two captures); 0xffff when idle.
fields.name: countdown_ticks

fields.description: Offsets 9-10, uint16 LE: the run length the device accepted.
fields.name: requested_seconds

parse_rules: Idle payload is 01 ff ff ff ff 00 00.
Offset 8 reads 0x40 while watering; whether it carries countdown bits for runs over 1023 s is unknown.

ProtobufStatus.description: Protobuf family: the decrypted inner message (aa 77 5a 0f <len LE16> <protobuf> <CRC LE16>) that answers get_status, a start, or the clock-sync message. Fields are protobuf field numbers; names are this document's own.

fields.description: Field 16 > field 1, enum: 0 off, 1 idle, 2 low battery (refuses to start watering), 3 rain delay, 4 watering, 5 mesh device offline.
fields.name: run_state

fields.description: Field 16 > 6 > 5, seconds left in the current run (counts down; present only while watering).
fields.name: seconds_remaining

fields.description: Field 16 > 6 > 7, total seconds of the current run (constant during the run).
fields.name: run_total

fields.description: Field 16 > 6 > 4, zero-based station running now (zone = value + 1).
fields.name: running_station

fields.description: Field 16 > 14 > 3, battery millivolts (also field 46 > 3 in the get_battery reply).
fields.name: battery_mv

fields.description: Top-level field 7, device clock, Unix epoch seconds UTC. Top-level field 1 carries the device's 6-byte MAC.
fields.name: device_clock

parse_rules: Verify the CRC-16/XMODEM (poly 0x1021, init 0, no reflection, no xor-out) over every byte before the CRC, stored little-endian; drop the message on mismatch.

The length field is a length (protobuf + 2), never a message type. Identify a message by which top-level protobuf field it carries: 16 status, 30 watering-status ack (field 1: 1 complete, 2 in progress, 3-7 delay states), 46 battery, 23 device info.
Decode the protobuf generically; field positions and lengths vary with content, so no fixed offsets exist.

envelope.handshake: Write 20 bytes C to 6c71 (random, C[11] = 0x00), read 20 bytes D. S = D[0:4] || C[4:20]. nonce = S[0:12]. ctr_tx = uint32 LE S[12:16]. ctr_rx = uint32 LE S[16:20]. Reject D whose first four bytes are all zero or whose bytes 4-19 are not all zero.
envelope.inner_message_protobuf_family: aa 77 5a 0f [length u16 LE = len(protobuf) + 2][protobuf][crc u16 LE]. CRC-16/XMODEM (poly 0x1021, init 0x0000, no reflection, no xor-out) over the header, length and protobuf — every byte before the CRC. (ljmerza's prose says "over the protobuf"; its code and all four captured requests checked here include the header.) Example: aa 77 5a 0f 04 00 7a 00 bc 34.
envelope.keystream: block_i = AES-128-ECB-encrypt(key, nonce || uint32 LE (ctr + i)). Ciphertext = plaintext XOR the keystream, truncated to the plaintext length. A frame of n bytes consumes ceil(n / 16) counter values; the next frame in the same direction starts at the following counter, and the unused tail of a partial block is discarded. Counters are per direction and per connection, never reset mid-connection. Counter wrap is modulo 2^32 in ljmerza (wxfield wraps at 2^32 - 1; never reached in practice).
envelope.outer_frame: [magic u8][len u8 = plaintext length][ciphertext][trailer u16 LE], total len + 4 bytes. magic 0x11 protobuf family, 0x10 HT25-0000. trailer = (magic + len + sum of PLAINTEXT bytes) mod 65536 — the additive sum of [magic, len] + plaintext, computed before encryption. Same rule on device-to-host frames.

frames.name: protobuf start_zone_2 600 s, second host frame (two blocks)
protobuf battery reply (minimal: field 46 {3: 2838 mV}), first device frame
HT25-0000 ht25_start, mesh id 0x1234, 600 s, first host frame of a fresh session

test_vectors.notes: Invented key, handshake and mesh id — no real unit. Computed by this project from the rules above; scripts/test_orbit_bhyve_ble_spec.py recomputes them.

published_inner_messages.notes: Plaintext requests from ljmerza docs/ble-messages.md; CRC-valid under the rule above.

ht25_mesh.battery_percent: Upstream's estimate only: 0 % at 2400 mV, 100 % at 3000 mV, linear, clamped.

init_sequence.notes: Sent in order, about 150 ms apart, after the handshake and before every watering command (ljmerza re-runs it per actuation; only steps 1-3 are confirmed necessary). Bodies follow the 5-byte header; <now> is <Unix seconds u32 LE><UTC offset minutes int16 LE>.
steps: type 0x85, message 0x00: 00 <hub mesh id LE16, 00 00 if no hub> 00 00 00 00

messages.0: configure device: write 01 <own mesh id LE16> 00 00 00 00 (set own id) or 00 <hub mesh id LE16> 00 00 00 00 (set server bridge id)
messages.1: device info: read with 00 00 00; reply <type u5 | hw u3> <firmware u16 LE, e.g. 85> <stations u6>
messages.13: watering control: 04 <seconds u16 LE> 00 00 00 00 start, 02 00 00 00 stop
messages.2: device status: read with 00; reply in payload_formats.Ht25Status
messages.24: watering delay end: write <until Unix seconds u32 LE>
messages.3: device health: read with seven zeros; reply on 6c73's format block
messages.5: UTC time: write <Unix seconds u32 LE><local offset minutes int16 LE>
messages.7: button preset run time: write <seconds u16 LE> (acked on fw0085)
messages.9: active programs bitmask; writing 00 disables every stored program (the app sends it on connect; upstream deliberately does not)

ht25_mesh.plaintext: [mesh id u16 LE][type u8][message id u16 LE][body]. type: bits 7-6 command (0 read, 1 read reply, 2 write, 3 write ack — the reply sets bit 0x40), bits 5-0 a sequence the device echoes. The message-id word: low 14 bits message id, top 2 bits destination; every frame observed carries destination 1, i.e. byte 4 = 0x40. No CRC, no protobuf; the outer trailer is the only check. Mesh id is the timer's own (credential:mesh_device_id); frames carrying another id are dropped silently. (Earlier notes called the first two bytes a fixed "d7 47" magic; that was one unit's mesh id.)

commands_used.clock_sync: Field 75 {1: Unix seconds UTC, 2: UTC offset seconds as int32 — negative values sign-extended to a 10-byte varint}. The vendor app sends it on connect and it elicits the same field-16 status as field 15; field 18 (ISO date string) does nothing over BLE.
commands_used.device_info_request: Field 22, empty (b2 01 00) -> field 23 {1: stations, 2: hardware string, 3: firmware string}.
commands_used.identify: Field 47 {1: seconds} flashes the LED on the Gen2 HT25G2 (latches; send 0 to stop); the XD ignores it.
commands_used.programs: Stored programs: field 19 writes a slot, field 20 {1: enable bitmask, program A = bit 0}, field 10 (empty) dumps every slot plus a status. A program runs only with the controller in auto. Out of scope here; see ljmerza docs/protocol.md.
commands_used.rain_delay: Field 17 {1: minutes, 3: end time Unix UTC, 4: 1}; {1: 0} cancels.
commands_used.skip_station: Field 21, empty: skip the zone running now (app behaviour; not hardware-verified upstream).
commands_used.timer_mode: Field 14 {1: mode (0 off, 1 auto, 2 manual), 2: manual parameters {3: station entry {1: zero-based station, 2: run seconds}}}. Field 2 must be present (empty for off/auto/stop). One station entry per run. General start body: 72 L1 08 02 12 L2 1a L3 08 <station varint> 10 <seconds varint>, with L3 = length of the station entry, L2 = L3 + 2, L1 = L2 + 4.

protobuf_family.flow: HT25G2 has a flow sensor: field 57 {1: interval ms, 2: duration s} subscribes, and field 59 frames stream ({1: frequency Hz, 3: cumulative ticks this run}); field 57 {1: 0} unsubscribes. A subscription left running persists across reconnects and starves status replies — always unsubscribe. Upstream bucket-measured about 433 ticks per US gallon.
protobuf_family.message: One protobuf message per inner message with exactly one top-level field set; the field number is the command. No .proto is needed: the bodies are small enough to encode by hand (tag = field << 3 | wire type; wire 0 varint, wire 2 length-delimited).

model_differences.HT25A-0001: fw0098: ignores run seconds (always 1800 s); stop_watering frame starts a run; stop with controller_off.
model_differences.HT31-0001: Single-station sibling of the XD (fw0058), hardware-verified on five units upstream.
model_differences.HT34-0001: Routed to the XD protocol on a fork's report; not hardware-tested by ljmerza.

protobuf_family.replies: A start is answered by a field-16 status; a stop by a bare field-30 watering-status ack only, so poll status to confirm. An idle timer pushes a status on connect; one that is watering or in rain delay often does not, so always request status explicitly.

transport_behaviour.duplicate_notifications: Drop a notification byte-identical to the previous one before decrypting (see 6c73 notes).
transport_behaviour.single_session: One central at a time. Upstream recommends connect, do one thing, disconnect, under a per-device lock.
transport_behaviour.write_mode: Write requests and write commands have both actuated an HT34A. ljmerza's current code writes with response (waiting under a second for it); its older docs/ble-protocol.md reports write requests of about 25 bytes or more refused with ATT error 0x80 on one unit, so fall back to write without response if that error appears.

remaining_unknowns: The schema cannot express this envelope: there is no framing scheme for AES-CTR with a handshake nonce, no CRC-16/XMODEM auto parameter, and no way to declare that a command body is wrapped in the inner aa775a0f message. Every command here is application plaintext that a client must pass through protocol_details.envelope; a consumer without a handler for it can describe the device but not drive it. `protocol_handler: bhyve_envelope` names the encoder a consumer needs; a declarative framing scheme would be the schema field that replaces it.

Protobuf-family status, battery and running zone come back as protobuf (payload_formats.ProtobufStatus) and have no fixed offsets, so no sensor or switch state is bound for those models. Battery is bound only for HT25-0000, whose health reply is fixed-layout.

Start durations on the protobuf family are bounded to 128-16383 s so the template's nested lengths stay fixed; shorter or longer runs are valid on the wire but need the lengths recomputed, which a template cannot do.

The family is chosen from the hardware string in the owner's account record (HT25…-0000 = mesh); the advertisement carries nothing that tells the families or models apart, so variants have no identification block.

The network key and mesh ids are only obtainable from the Orbit account (or the vendor app's storage on a rooted phone). If the cloud is retired before an owner exports them, no public method recovers them.
Whether the outer trailer is enforced by the device (sources disagree; see evidence).
Factory reset procedure and whether it clears the mesh key.
HT34-0001 and HT32A-0001 actuation rests on sibling-model evidence; HT25-0001 (bare) is routed to the protobuf family by rule, not by a tested unit.
HT25-0000 STATUS countdown: 1/64 s ticks is a fit to two captures; runs over 1023 s may use offset 8.

characteristics.name: Session handshake
characteristics.notes: 20-byte write then 20-byte read, once per connection; see `initialization`. Absent when the timer is in its bootloader.

controller_auto.description: Protobuf family: controller mode auto (stored programs run) — timerMode {mode 1, empty manualModeParams}. The empty field 2 is required; a timerMode without it is silently ignored.

controller_off.description: Protobuf family: controller mode off — timerMode {mode 0, empty manualModeParams}. Stops a run on every model and is the only verified stop on HT25A-0001 fw0098. It also disables stored programs until controller_auto is sent; upstream sends controller_auto after a stop if the controller was in auto before.

get_battery.description: Protobuf family: empty field-45 battery request; the reply is field 46 {field 3 battery millivolts}. Inner message aa 77 5a 0f 05 00 ea 02 00 dd 7e, as captured upstream.

get_status.description: Protobuf family: empty field-15 status request; the device answers with a field-16 status message (run state, seconds remaining, running station, battery mV). Laid out in payload_formats.ProtobufStatus. Inner message aa 77 5a 0f 04 00 7a 00 bc 34, as captured upstream.

ht25_read_health.description: HT25-0000: device-health read (mesh message 3). The reply carries the timer's local clock, battery millivolts and fault bits; laid out on 00006c73-fe32-4f58-8b78-98e42b2c047f. Also step 3 of the mesh init, so every init yields a battery reading.

mesh_id.description: This timer's own mesh device id.

ht25_read_status.description: HT25-0000: device-status read (mesh message 2); reply in payload_formats.Ht25Status. Also step 2 of the mesh init.

mesh_id.description: This timer's own mesh device id.

ht25_start.description: HT25-0000: open the valve for `duration` seconds. Mesh header [mesh id LE16][0xb6][0x0d 0x40] then 04 <seconds LE16> 00 00 00 00. For mesh id 0x1234 and 600 s the plaintext is 34 12 b6 0d 40 04 58 02 00 00 00 00. Run the mesh init first in the same connection. The device acks with type byte 0xf6 echoing 04 <seconds>.

duration.description: Run time in seconds. 600 s is the app's default manual run.

mesh_id.description: This timer's own mesh device id; a frame carrying another id is ignored without error.

ht25_stop.description: HT25-0000: close the valve. Header [mesh id LE16][0xb7][0x0d 0x40] then 02 00 00 00. Ack type byte 0xf7. Run the mesh init first in the same connection.

mesh_id.description: This timer's own mesh device id.

start_zone_1.description: Protobuf family: manual run of zone 1 (wire station 0) for `duration` seconds — field 14 timerMode {mode 2 manual, field 2 manualModeParams {field 3 stationInfo {field 1 station 0, field 2 run seconds}}}. 600 s renders as the body 72 0b 08 02 12 07 1a 05 08 00 10 d8 04. HT25A-0001 fw0098 ignores the duration (see its entity).

duration.description: Run time in seconds, protobuf varint. Bounded to 128-16383 so the varint is exactly two bytes and the nested lengths in the template hold; any other value needs the lengths recomputed (protocol_details.protobuf_family). The device's own maximum is not known.

start_zone_2.description: As start_zone_1 for zone 2 (wire station 1). HT32A, HT34A and HT34 only.

duration.description: Run time in seconds; two-byte varint range, as start_zone_1.

start_zone_3.description: As start_zone_1 for zone 3 (wire station 2). HT34A and HT34 only.

duration.description: Run time in seconds; two-byte varint range, as start_zone_1.

start_zone_4.description: As start_zone_1 for zone 4 (wire station 3). HT34A and HT34 only.

duration.description: Run time in seconds; two-byte varint range, as start_zone_1.

stop_watering.description: Protobuf family: stop whatever is running — timerMode {mode 2 manual, empty manualModeParams}. Verified upstream on HT25G2-0001 fw0111 and HT34A-0001 fw0107. NOT for HT25A-0001 fw0098, where this exact frame STARTS a default 30-minute run; use controller_off there. The device answers a stop with a bare field-30 ack and no status, so read status afterwards to confirm.

characteristics.name: Encrypted command (host to device)
characteristics.notes: NOTHING HERE IS WRITTEN RAW. The commands below are application plaintext; protocol_details.envelope turns each one into the bytes written: (protobuf family only) wrap the protobuf body as aa 77 5a 0f <len LE16 = body + 2> <body> <CRC-16/XMODEM LE over everything before it>; then XOR with the AES-128 keystream at the host-to-device counter; then frame as <magic> <len u8> <ciphertext> <trailer LE16 = (magic + len + sum(plaintext)) mod 65536>, magic 0x11 for the protobuf family and 0x10 for HT25-0000. Commands whose name starts ht25_ are for HT25-0000; the rest are protobuf bodies for every other model. Upstream writes with response but caps the wait under a second (an ESPHome proxy never relays the response); the real acknowledgement is a notification. A frame with a malformed or unknown protobuf field gets no reply and desyncs the device's counter for the rest of the connection — reconnect.

format.name: mesh_id
format.notes: The timer's own mesh device id.

format.name: type
format.notes: Bits 7-6 command (1 = read reply), bits 5-0 sequence.

format.name: device_clock
format.notes: The timer's local time, seconds since the Unix epoch in local time.

format.name: battery_mv
format.notes: Battery voltage of the AA pack. Upstream accepts 1500-4000 and matched the cloud's figure to within 1 mV on three units. Upstream's percent is a linear 2400 mV = 0 % to 3000 mV = 100 % approximation for alkaline cells, not a device value.

format.name: fault_flags
format.notes: Bit 0 voltage-boost circuit fail, bit 1 valve on but no flow, bit 2 valve off but flow (leak).

format_match.notes: Mesh message id 3 (device health). Check also that byte 4 is 0x40 and bit 0x40 of byte 2 is set (a reply).

characteristics.name: Encrypted reply (device to host)
characteristics.notes:
Every reply arrives here as <magic> <len> <ciphertext> <trailer>, decrypted with the device-to-host counter, which runs as one continuous stream across notifications. Drop a notification that is byte-identical to the previous one before decrypting it: a proxy can re-deliver frames, and decrypting a duplicate advances the counter and corrupts every later frame (protobuf replies then fail their CRC — the signal to reconnect). A long protobuf reply arrives as several frames; concatenate the decrypted payloads and split on the aa 77 5a 0f header.
The layout below is the HT25-0000 device-health reply (decrypted offsets). The other mesh replies and the protobuf status are in payload_formats. Protobuf-family plaintext starts aa 77 5a 0f, so offset 3 is 0x0f there and this matcher does not fire on a protobuf message's first frame.

characteristics.name: Unused write characteristic
characteristics.notes: Answers ATT error 0x80 / "write not permitted" to every write tried upstream. ljmerza associates it with the firmware path. Do not write it.

services.name: B-hyve timer service
services.notes: Handle numbers vary between units; address characteristics by UUID. Upstream requests a larger ATT MTU (the app asks for about 262; 247 is plenty) so a reply of up to ~100 bytes arrives in one notification.
